questions.stem: Write down the values of \(x\) for which the parabola \(y = (x+2)(x-2)\) is below the \(x\)-axis.

List all distinct pairs satisfying the conditions.

Equate the total fencing used to the available length of 60 m.

questions.stem: Find the value of \(k\) for which the quadratic function \(y = x^2 + 12x + k\) has exactly one zero.
questions.hint: Set the discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) to zero and solve for k.
questions.solution: The quadratic has exactly one zero when \(\Delta = 0\). Thus, \(12^2 - 4(1)(k) = 0 \implies 144 = 4k \implies k = 36\).

questions.solution: For no zeroes, \(\Delta < 0 \implies 8^2 - 4(\lambda-2)(4) < 0 \implies 64 - 16(\lambda-2) < 0 \implies 64 - 16\lambda + 32 < 0 \implies 96 - 16\lambda < 0 \implies \lambda > 6\).

questions.stem: Determine the discriminant \(\Delta\), then solve \(\Delta = 0\) to find the values of \(g\) for which the quadratic function \(y = gx^2 - 10x + g\) has exactly one zero.
questions.hint: Set the discriminant to zero to find the values of g.
questions.solution: The discriminant is \(\Delta = (-10)^2 - 4(g)(g) = 100 - 4g^2\). Set \(\Delta = 0 \implies 100 - 4g^2 = 0 \implies g^2 = 25 \implies g = \pm 5\).

Equate the discriminant to zero for exactly one zero.

questions.stem: Determine the discriminant \(\Delta\), then solve \(\Delta = 0\) to find the values of \(g\) for which the quadratic function \(y = 4x^2 + 2gx + (2g - 3)\) has exactly one zero.
questions.hint: Equate the discriminant expression to zero and factorise the quadratic equation in g.
questions.solution: The discriminant is \(\Delta = (2g)^2 - 4(4)(2g-3) = 4g^2 - 16(2g-3) = 4(g^2 - 8g + 12)\). Set \(\Delta = 0 \implies g^2 - 8g + 12 = 0 \implies (g-2)(g-6) = 0 \implies g = 2 \text{ or } g = 6\).

steps.explain: Determine the discriminant \(\Delta\) of the function.

questions.hint: Set the discriminant expression equal to zero and solve for g.
questions.solution: The discriminant is \(\Delta = [-2(g+2)]^2 - 4(4)(9) = 4(g+2)^2 - 144\). Set \(\Delta = 0 \implies 4(g+2)^2 = 144 \implies (g+2)^2 = 36 \implies g+2 = \pm 6 \implies g = 4 \text{ or } g = -8\).

questions.stem: Determine the discriminant \(\Delta\), then solve \(\Delta = 0\) to find the values of \(g\) for which the quadratic function \(y = (2g - 1)x^2 + (4g - 1)x + (2g + 1)\) has exactly one zero.

questions.stem:
Consider the following quadratic equations, where \(\lambda\) is a real number.

(i) \(x^2+\lambda x-2=0\)

(ii) \(x^2+(\lambda+2)x+(\lambda-3)=0\)

parts.stem: Prove that the roots of each equation are real and distinct for all real values of \(\lambda\).
parts.answer:
(i) \(\Delta=\lambda^2-4(1)(-2)=\lambda^2+8\ge8>0\), because \(\lambda^2\ge0\) for every real \(\lambda\).
(ii) \(\Delta=(\lambda+2)^2-4(1)(\lambda-3)=\lambda^2+4\lambda+4-4\lambda+12=\lambda^2+16\ge16>0\).
Both discriminants are positive for every real \(\lambda\), so each equation has two real and distinct roots.
Marking guide (3 marks): 1 correct discriminant for (i) with the reason it is positive; 1 correct discriminant for (ii), expanded and simplified to \(\lambda^2+16\), with the reason it is positive; 1 conclusion that holds for all real \(\lambda\).

steps.explain: A quadratic \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) has two real and distinct roots exactly when its discriminant \(\Delta=b^2-4ac\) is positive. So we must show \(\Delta>0\) for every real \(\lambda\), for BOTH equations.
Equation (i): \(x^2+\lambda x-2=0\). Read off \(a=1\), \(b=\lambda\), \(c=-2\) and substitute.
The square of any real number is never negative, so \(\lambda^2\ge0\). Adding 8 makes \(\Delta_1\) at least 8, which is positive whatever \(\lambda\) is.
Equation (ii): \(x^2+(\lambda+2)x+(\lambda-3)=0\). Here \(a=1\), \(b=\lambda+2\), \(c=\lambda-3\). Square the bracket carefully and distribute the \(-4\) over \((\lambda-3)\).
Again \(\lambda^2\ge0\), so \(\Delta_2\) is at least 16, which is positive for every real \(\lambda\).

Conclusion: \(\Delta_1>0\) and \(\Delta_2>0\) for every real \(\lambda\), so both equations have two real and distinct roots whatever the value of \(\lambda\). Quick check: \(\lambda=0\) gives \(\Delta_1=8\) and \(\Delta_2=16\); \(\lambda=-2\) gives \(\Delta_1=12\) and \(\Delta_2=20\), all positive.

(ii) \(\Delta=(\lambda+2)^2-4(1)(\lambda-3)=\lambda^2+4\lambda+4-4\lambda+12=\lambda^2+16\ge16>0\).
Both discriminants are positive for every real \(\lambda\), so each equation has two real and distinct roots.

parts.stem: In the case of equation (i) \(x^2 + \lambda x - 2 = 0\), use the concavity and y-intercept of the associated parabola to give an alternative explanation for why the roots are real and distinct.
parts.answer:
The parabola \(y=x^2+\lambda x-2\) has a positive coefficient of \(x^2\), so it is concave up.
Its y-intercept is \(y=-2\), which is below the x-axis, for every value of \(\lambda\).
A concave-up parabola that passes through a point below the x-axis must rise above the axis on both sides of that point, so it crosses the x-axis twice (once on each side of the y-axis). Two x-intercepts means two real and distinct roots.
Marking guide (3 marks): 1 concave up because the coefficient of \(x^2\) is positive; 1 y-intercept is \(-2<0\); 1 conclusion that the curve crosses the x-axis twice, so there are two real distinct roots.

steps.explain: Concavity. The associated parabola is \(y=x^2+\lambda x-2\). The coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(1\), which is positive, so the parabola opens upwards (concave up) for every value of \(\lambda\). The graph shows two examples, \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=-3\).

y-intercept. Put \(x=0\). The \(\lambda x\) term disappears, so the y-intercept is \(-2\) whatever \(\lambda\) is. Every one of these parabolas passes through the point \((0,-2)\), which lies below the x-axis (highlighted).

Put the two facts together. A concave-up parabola rises without limit on both the far left and the far right. Since it passes through \((0,-2)\) below the axis, it must cross the x-axis once to the left of the y-axis and once to the right: exactly two x-intercepts (the green points).

Conclusion. Two x-intercepts mean two real and distinct roots, for every real \(\lambda\). This agrees with part (a), where \(\Delta_1=\lambda^2+8>0\). It also agrees with the product of the roots \(\dfrac{c}{a}=-2<0\), which shows one root is positive and one is negative.

questions.stem: Consider the problem of finding the number of intersections between a line (e.g., \\(x - y + 2 = 0\\)) and a circle centered at the origin (e.g., \\(x^2 + y^2 = 9\\)). Instead of substituting the line equation into the circle equation and using the discriminant, how could this be solved using geometry? (Hint: Consider the perpendicular distance from the center of the circle to the line.)
options: Calculate the perpendicular distance from the center of the circle (1,0) to the line and compare it to the radius.
Calculate the perpendicular distance from the center of the circle (0,0) to the line and compare it to the radius.
Calculate the perpendicular distance from the center of the circle (-1,0) to the line and compare it to the radius.
questions.hint: Use the perpendicular distance formula from a point to a line to compare the distance with the circle's radius.
questions.solution: The perpendicular distance \(d\) from the origin \((0,0)\) to the line \(Ax + By + C = 0\) is \(d = \frac{|C|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}\). If \(d < r\), it intersects twice. If \(d = r\), it is tangent. If \(d > r\), it does not intersect.

steps.explain: State the geometric criterion for circle-line intersection: calculate the perpendicular distance \(d\) from the center \((0,0)\) to the line.
For part a (circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 9\) with radius \(r = 3\) and line \(x - y + 2 = 0\)), compute the perpendicular distance.
Compare the distance \(d\) to the radius \(r\). Since \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 < 3\), the line is closer to the center than the boundary, so it intersects twice.
For part b i (circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 2\) with radius \(r = \sqrt{2}\) and line \(x - y + 3 = 0\)), compute the perpendicular distance.
Compare the distance \(d\) to the radius \(r\). Since \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} = 1.5\sqrt{2} > \sqrt{2}\), the line is further from the center than the radius, so they do not intersect.

questions.stem: Determine the values of \(p\), \(q\), and \(r\) so that \(2x^2 - 4x + 6 = px^2 + q(x-1)^2 + r(x-2)^2\) for all values of \(x\).
questions.hint: Expand the right side and equate the coefficients of like terms.
questions.solution: Expand the RHS to get \((p+q+r)x^2 - (2q+4r)x + (q+4r)\). Equating coefficients with the LHS yields \(q+4r = 6\), \(2q+4r = 4\), and \(p+q+r = 2\). Solving this system gives \(p=2, q=-2, r=2\).

questions.stem: As a sphere of radius \(r\) is being heated, it expands such that its surface area \(S\) is increasing at a constant rate of \(1.5\ \text{mm}^2\text{s}^{-1}\). Show that \(\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac{3}{16\pi r}\).
